subtitle: Reading passages on the rise of Islam, the Golden Age, and Islamic civilisation's legacy.

data.sourceTitle: The Rise of Islam and the Early Caliphates
data.targetTitle: The Rise of Islam and the Early Caliphates
data.sourcePassage:
Islam began in western Arabia in the 7th century. The Prophet Muhammad was born in Mecca around 570 CE. According to Islamic belief, Muhammad received revelations from God beginning in 610 CE. These revelations were later written down to form the Qur'an, Islam's holy book. Muhammad's message faced opposition in Mecca, and in 622 CE he and his followers moved to Medina. This event is called the Hijra and marks the start of the Islamic calendar.

After Muhammad's death in 632 CE, the Muslim community needed new leadership. Rulers called caliphs took charge, claiming authority over the growing Muslim world. The first major dynasty was the Umayyad Caliphate, which ruled from 661 to 750 CE. The Umayyads expanded Islamic rule across North Africa, into Iberia (modern Spain and Portugal) and eastwards into Central Asia. Their capital was Damascus in Syria.

In 750 CE, the Abbasid dynasty replaced the Umayyads. The Abbasids founded a new capital at Baghdad in 762 CE. Baghdad was carefully positioned near the Tigris River, close to trade routes linking the Mediterranean, Persia, Arabia and the Indian Ocean. It grew into one of the most important cities of the medieval world.

Historians note that the spread of Islamic rule did not mean everyone instantly became Muslim. Conversion happened at different speeds in different places. Many people remained Christian, Jewish, Zoroastrian, Hindu or followed other beliefs. In most areas, Muslim rulers governed diverse, mixed populations.

questions.question: What was the Hijra?
options: The revelation of the Qur'an to Muhammad
Muhammad's move from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE
The founding of Baghdad
The defeat of the Umayyad Caliphate
questions.modelAnswer: The Hijra was Muhammad's move from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE. It marks the start of the Islamic calendar and helped establish the first Muslim community with political importance.

questions.question: Which dynasty founded Baghdad as its capital in 762 CE?
options: The Umayyads
The Fatimids
The Abbasids
The Mongols
questions.modelAnswer: The Abbasids founded Baghdad in 762 CE after replacing the Umayyad dynasty in 750 CE. Baghdad's location near the Tigris River made it a vital centre of trade and learning.

questions.question: Why does the passage suggest that the Umayyad Caliphate was historically significant?
options: It was the first caliphate to found Baghdad
It expanded Islamic rule across North Africa, Iberia and Central Asia
It translated Greek texts into Arabic
It created the Islamic calendar
questions.modelAnswer: The Umayyad Caliphate was significant because it greatly expanded the territory under Islamic rule, spreading across North Africa, Iberia and Central Asia between 661 and 750 CE, connecting many diverse peoples and regions.

questions.question: What does the passage suggest about the relationship between Islamic rule and religious conversion?
options: All people under Islamic rule converted to Islam immediately
Conversion was forbidden under the Umayyad Caliphate
Conversion happened at different speeds and many people kept other faiths
Only Arabs were permitted to convert to Islam
questions.modelAnswer: The passage states that the spread of Islamic rule did not mean everyone instantly became Muslim. Conversion happened at different speeds and many people remained Christian, Jewish, Zoroastrian, Hindu or followed other beliefs. This shows that Islamic-ruled societies were religiously diverse.

data.sourceTitle: The Islamic Golden Age: Science, Medicine and Culture
data.targetTitle: The Islamic Golden Age: Science, Medicine and Culture
data.sourcePassage:
Between roughly the 700s and the 1200s CE, cities such as Baghdad, Cordoba and Cairo became remarkable centres of scholarship, science and culture. Historians sometimes call this period the Islamic Golden Age, though they debate whether the label is fully accurate because it can hide diversity and change.

One of the most significant developments was the translation movement in Baghdad. Scholars translated works from Greek, Persian, Sanskrit and Syriac into Arabic. They did not simply copy. They discussed, corrected, criticised and expanded earlier knowledge. Arabic became an important language of scholarship across many regions, not only among Arab scholars.

In mathematics, scholars worked with Indian numerals, algebra and geometry. Al-Khwarizmi wrote influential works on calculation and algebra — the word 'algebra' itself comes from the Arabic title of one of his books. In medicine, Ibn Sina (known in Latin Europe as Avicenna) wrote The Canon of Medicine, which was studied in Islamic and European universities for centuries. In geography, Al-Idrisi created an important world map while working at a Christian court in Sicily, showing that knowledge exchange crossed religious and political boundaries.

Astronomy was especially important. Scholars observed the sky, improved instruments such as the astrolabe, and created tables showing the movements of stars and planets. Astronomy helped with calendars, navigation and working out prayer times.

Scholarship was supported by rulers, wealthy patrons, libraries and manuscript copying. Paper-making, which had spread from China through Central Asia, made books easier to produce and store. These conditions — alongside trade routes that carried scholars, books and instruments across Afro-Eurasia — made the Golden Age possible.

questions.question: What does the word 'algebra' show about Islamic scholarship?
options: It proves all mathematics was invented in Baghdad
It shows the Arabic language influenced later mathematics
It was a form of religious writing
It was only used in Cordoba
questions.modelAnswer: The word 'algebra' comes from the Arabic title of one of Al-Khwarizmi's books. This shows that Islamic scholarship made lasting contributions to mathematics whose influence can still be seen in the language we use today.

questions.question: Which of the following was an important use of astronomy in Islamic-ruled societies?
options: Planning military campaigns
Calculating the direction of Mecca and prayer times
Designing mosques
Writing poetry
questions.modelAnswer: Astronomy helped Islamic scholars work out prayer times and the direction of Mecca, as well as supporting calendars and navigation. This made it both a religious and a practical science.

questions.question: What does Al-Idrisi's work at a Christian court in Sicily suggest about medieval knowledge exchange?
options: Islamic and Christian civilisations never cooperated
Knowledge exchange crossed religious and political boundaries
Only Muslim scholars produced geographical works
Sicily was always part of the Islamic world
questions.modelAnswer: Al-Idrisi, a Muslim geographer, created an important world map while working at the Christian court of Roger II in Sicily. This shows that knowledge exchange happened across religious and political boundaries, with scholars working in different cultural settings.

questions.question: Why do historians debate whether the label 'Islamic Golden Age' is fully accurate?
options: Because no scholars actually lived in Baghdad
Because the period saw no achievements in science or culture
Because the label can hide diversity, conflict and change across different regions
Because the achievements only benefited Arab Muslims
questions.modelAnswer: Historians debate the 'Islamic Golden Age' label because it can suggest all Islamic-ruled societies were equally wealthy and peaceful, which was not true. It can over-focus on Baghdad and hide the contributions of Cairo, Cordoba, Samarkand and Timbuktu. It can also hide conflict, inequality, slavery and change over time.

data.sourceTitle: The Impact and Legacy of Islamic Civilisations
data.targetTitle: The Impact and Legacy of Islamic Civilisations
data.sourcePassage:
Islamic civilisations had a major impact on the wider world, not only in the medieval period but in ways that continued into later centuries. This influence can be traced through trade, scholarship, architecture and cultural exchange.

Trade routes were central to Islamic civilisations' global reach. Merchants travelled across the Mediterranean, the Sahara, the Indian Ocean and the Silk Roads, carrying goods such as spices, textiles, gold, salt, books and paper. These routes carried more than goods — they moved languages, religious ideas, medical knowledge, mathematical methods and artistic styles.

The legacy of Islamic scholarship was also lasting. Works translated into Arabic were later translated into Latin and other European languages, helping shape learning in medieval Europe. The ideas of Ibn Sina, Al-Razi and Al-Khwarizmi influenced medicine and mathematics long after the peak Abbasid period. Arabic numerals, adopted across the Islamic world from Indian sources, spread to Europe and remain in global use today.

In architecture, the legacy of Islamic civilisations can be seen in mosques, palaces and decorative styles that influenced art and building across Asia, Africa and Europe. Geometric patterns, arabesques, domed buildings and calligraphy became associated with Islamic artistic traditions.

Historians also note that studying Islamic civilisations challenges the idea that medieval history was mainly a European story. Islamic-ruled societies were deeply connected to African, Asian and European worlds. Cities such as Baghdad, Cairo, Cordoba, Samarkand and Timbuktu show that great centres of power, trade and learning existed across Afro-Eurasia — not only in western Europe.

Nothing beyond basic food and clothing

options: Ancient Rome
Greece
India
China

Through geometric patterns, arabesques, domed buildings and calligraphy that spread across Asia, Africa and Europe

questions.question: What argument does the passage make about the importance of studying Islamic civilisations for KS3 history students?
options: That Islamic civilisations were superior to all other medieval societies
That studying Islamic civilisations challenges the Eurocentric view of medieval history and shows Afro-Eurasian connections
That the only relevant medieval civilisation was located in Baghdad
That medieval history is mainly about conflict between Christians and Muslims
